entries.topic: Money fixes: public financing, disclosure, lobbying limits, amendment; NRSC v. FEC

claims.text: NYC matches contributions up to $250 at $8 to $1; 94% of candidates in the 2021 primary took part

Malbin and Parrott (2017): NYC council races small donors per 100,000 constituents rose from 176 (1:1 match, 1997) to 218 (6:1, 2009-13); small donors' share of funds rose from 45% to 63%; LA's program showed no meaningful gain (174 to 161); difference-in-differences vs state assembly districts significant for NYC; 73% of NYC census block groups had $100-250 donors vs 43%/57% in LA; mayoral races drew smaller, less diverse small-donor shares

Seattle: four $25 vouchers per resident each cycle, property-levy funded ($3M/yr; Prop 1 raises $4.5M/yr for 10 years); users 38,000 (6.76% of voting-age residents) 2019, 48,000 (7.59%) 2021, 30,649 (4.72%) 2023; Georgetown/Stony Brook study: users skew higher-income, white, older but 'more representative of all Seattle voters than cash donors'; critic Ari Hoffman: 'inefficient, underutilized, and fails to curb big money's influence'; PACs spent over $2M on the 2021 mayoral race
Seattle Proposition 1 (renewal of the Democracy Voucher levy) passed 59.12% to 40.88% on 5 August 2025

Presidential public funding began with the 1976 cycle; Obama in 2008 was the first major-party nominee to decline public funds entirely; in 2012 neither Obama nor Romney accepted; checkoff participation peaked at 28.7% (1980), about 6% in 2012; spending limits regarded as 'too low to permit effective campaigning'

DISCLOSE Act of 2026 introduced 4 March 2026 by Whitehouse, Pappas, Raskin and Morelle with 186 Democrats (all 47 senators caucusing with Democrats, 139 House Democrats); groups spending over $10,000 on elections must disclose donors over $10,000; bars transfers to hide donors; extends disclaimers online
DISCLOSE Act (S.4822) cloture on the motion to proceed failed 49-49 on 22 September 2022

Blanes i Vidal, Draca and Fons-Rosen (AER 2012): lobbyists who had worked for a US senator 'suffer a 24 percent drop' in revenue when that senator leaves office; drop immediate, lasting, larger for senior/powerful senators; read as evidence lobbyists sell access

NRSC v. FEC, decided 30 June 2026: FECA limits on political parties' coordinated expenditures violate the First Amendment; Colorado II (2001) overruled; parties may now coordinate unlimited spending with candidates; rules for super PACs and 501(c)(4)s unchanged; parties still cannot accept corporate contributions
NRSC v. FEC: 6-3, Kavanaugh for the Court; Kagan dissenting, joined by Sotomayor and Jackson

Americans for Prosperity Foundation v. Bonta, 1 July 2021, 6-3 (Roberts): California's requirement that charities file their major donors with the state burdened donors' First Amendment rights and was not narrowly tailored; Roberts: California 'casts a dragnet for sensitive donor information'; the ACLU, NAACP Legal Defense Fund and Human Rights Campaign backed the challengers; Sotomayor (with Breyer, Kagan) dissented, warning of a 'significant risk that it will topple disclosure regimes that should be constitutional'

entries.topic: Structure fixes: NPV compact law, commissions, top-two, term limits, AVR, votes at 16

claims.text: NPVIC debate: critics argue it needs congressional consent under the Compact Clause, that it would remove House contingent elections, that its six-month withdrawal blackout may conflict with the Presidential Electors Clause (von Spakovsky), that replacing the EC requires an Article V amendment (Drake and others), and that it raises equal-protection (Williams) and VRA (Gringer) problems; supporters (Akhil and Vikram Amar, Raskin) cite states' plenary power to appoint electors; Akhil Amar argues it creates no new interstate apparatus

Arizona State Legislature v. AIRC, 29 June 2015, 5-4 (Ginsburg; Roberts dissent with Scalia, Thomas, Alito): the Elections Clause permits voters to create a redistricting commission by initiative; Arizona's commission created by Proposition 106 (2000); five members, four chosen by legislative leaders, who pick a fifth; Ballotpedia lists eight states with independent commissions (AK, AZ, CA, ID, MT, WA, CO, MI)

Nelson (PS 2023), US House elections 1982-2018: relative to legislative redistricting, independent commissions associated with lower odds of incumbent-party wins (odds ratio 0.48) and higher odds of competitive (45-55%) elections (2.25); political commissions not significant; association not causation; incumbent party has won 94% of congressional elections since the 2010 cycle; California competitive districts 5.2% before commission to 14.6% after

FairVote (2013): California's commission produced more legitimate but not more competitive lines; competitive districts 5 in both 2008 and 2012; turnover in 2012 inflated by one-time incumbent pairings; partisan sorting cited
California Proposition 50, approved 65%-35% on 4 November 2025, allowed a legislature-adopted replacement congressional map through 2030, aimed at five more Democratic-leaning seats

McGhee and Shor (2017): 'We find an inconsistent effect' of the top-two primary in California and Washington; some moderation in California among Democrats, partly coinciding with new commission lines and term limits; 'virtually no effect of the Top Two in Washington'

Massachusetts Question 3 (3 Nov 2026 ballot, certified 17 July 2026): single top-two primary for most state and congressional offices (presidential primary excluded), effective 1 Jan 2028; Yes on 3 (Coalition for Healthy Democracy) about $7.16M raised to 20 Oct 2026, opposition about $195,000; supporters include Reps. Auchincloss and Moulton, Auditor DiZoglio, ex-Govs Baker (R) and Patrick (D); opponents include the state Democratic and Republican parties, Working Families Party, Sen. Markey, Rep. Pressley, Mayor Wu; suit Jackson v. Coalition for Healthy Democracy filed

NCSL/CSG/SLLF joint project (reported Aug 2006): term limits weakened legislatures relative to governors, increased reliance on lobbyists and staff, reduced cross-party civility; female representation fell in most term-limited legislatures; Kurtz: term limits 'have done more to limit rather than enhance the effectiveness of the legislative branch'; 'The public doesn't have much of an appetite for repeal'

U.S. Term Limits v. Thornton (1995), 5-4 (Stevens): states may not add to the Constitution's qualifications for Congress, so state-imposed congressional term limits are unconstitutional; nearly half the states had sought such limits

Gronke et al. for the Center for American Progress (2017): Oregon's automatic registration added about 116,000 people unlikely to register otherwise, of whom about 40,000 voted in Nov 2016 (projections); new registrants younger, more diverse, lower-income and rural; OPB called it 'a relatively modest' increase
Seljan, Lochner and Webb (Electoral Studies 2023): Oregon back-end AVR registrants had a 66% lower rate of party registration; 'very little partisan mobilization occurs following registration'

California DMV motor-voter system: about 23,000 registration errors disclosed Sept 2018 and about 1,500 more wrongful registrations including non-citizens (Oct 2018); Secretary of State Padilla 'deeply frustrated and disappointed', sought an independent audit; registrations cancelled; no report that any wrongly registered person voted

Takoma Park lowered its voting age to 16 for city elections in 2013, the first US jurisdiction to do so; turnout of 16-17-year-olds vs all voters: 44% vs 10% (2013), about 45% vs 21% (2015), about 48% vs 22% (2017), 69% vs 54% (2020; 132 of 191 registered)

Nov 2020: Oakland Measure QQ (16-year-olds vote for school board) passed; San Francisco Prop G narrowly failed, a similar 2016 measure lost by 4 points; California Prop 18 (17-year-olds in primaries) lost by 10 points; the San Francisco Chronicle opposed Prop G as inconsistent with higher ages for smoking and military service
